title: Capacity Sundial: Adaptive Windows & Tenant Priming (PRD draft)
body:
Summary:

This is a working PRD draft for a feature set we’re calling "Capacity Sundial": an adaptive time-windowing approach to Dedicated capacity autoscaling that pairs short-term micro-reservoirs ("pulses") with tenant priming and graceful soft-decommit semantics. The goal is to let tenants get transient burst throughput without compromising long-tail latency SLOs or tenant isolation guarantees.

Why this problem now:
- Customers want lower-per-token cost through opportunistic capacity while keeping predictable latency and no noisy-neighbor regressions.
- Existing approaches (simple lane-based burst credits, large warm pools) either waste capacity or expose other tenants to risk during sudden spikes.
- We need a solution that is workload-aware, time-local, and operationally straightforward for Dedicated and Private deployments.

Product goals (what success looks like):
- Reduce 95th/99th token-latency regressions during multi-tenant bursts by >= 30% compared to naive shared warm pool baseline.
- Provide transient burst capacity for small-to-medium bursts (up to 3x baseline for 1-10 minutes) for at least 80% of eligible tenants without requiring committed capacity increases.
- Ensure tenant isolation: no tenant should cause another tenant’s latency SLO to breach more than 1% of incidents in a quarter.
- Operational cost impact: additional reserved prewarm compute should be <= 8% of total Dedicated pool capacity on average across mixed workloads.

Non-goals:
- This does not replace long-term reserved capacity planning or scheduled seasonal provisioning.
- Not intended to handle multi-hour flash-surge smoothing (that remains a separate seasonality autoscale policy).

User personas & stories:
- Platform engineer (SRE): wants predictable fallbacks and easy-to-debug degradation routes when pulses are exhausted.
- Tenant product owner (AI infra): wants quick, short bursts for sudden traffic without buying more reserved GPUs.
- Operator (Support): wants clear runbooks and metrics to answer customer questions about why a burst was rejected or throttled.

Key concepts (terminology):
- Sundial window: a short adaptive time window (default 1m, adjustable 30s–5m) used to compute transient headroom and prewarm cadence.
- Pulse (micro-reservoir): a small, rolling pool of warmed instances/kernels reserved for transient bursts; replenished according to predictive heuristics.
- Tenant Priming: low-cost prewarming actions targeted at a single tenant (e.g., keep small KV cache, prefix cache, and one lightweight worker warm) based on recent usage or predicted demand.
- Soft-decommit: a graceful pathway to free prewarm resources by throttling or shifting traffic to lower-cost model variants rather than abrupt eviction.

Functional requirements (high level):
1) Adaptive sundial windows per pool: compute dynamic windows based on incoming burstiness signals and sequence-length distribution.
2) Pulse allocator: maintain per-pool and per-tenant pulse quotas; pulses are small fractions of full instance counts and can be transiently borrowed.
3) Priming policy engine: decide which tenants receive priming budget based on history, ML predictor, and explicit entitlement (enterprise tiers).
4) Soft-decommit flows: when reclaiming pulse resources, trigger step-down actions: a) reduce per-request concurrency, b) route to quantized/cheaper model variant, c) throttle with informative error codes.
5) Isolation fences: strict enforcement that ensures borrowings can't reduce other tenants’ guaranteed capacity below configured SLO thresholds.
6) Metrics/telemetry: expose token-level latency percentiles per-tenant, pulse consumption, priming hits/misses, and reclaim events.

Non-functional requirements:
- Latency SLO preservation: any scheduler decisions must respect per-tenant latency budgets at 95th/99th percentile (configurable).
- Determinism & explainability: operator should be able to reconstruct why a pulse was granted/revoked within a 10-second window.
- Backward compatibility: default behavior is opt-in (tenants enable pulse/priming); disabled tenants behave as today.

Proposed design (conceptual):
1) Observability input: collect short-window traffic features (rps delta, median seq length, KV hit-rate) into a rolling 30s aggregator.
2) Predictive scorer: a lightweight EWMA + classifier that outputs pulse-allocation probability and priming score per tenant.
3) Sundial controller: for each Dedicated pool, compute an adaptive window size and target pulse capacity = pool_capacity * window_factor * burst_sensitivity.
4) Pulse lifecycle: allocate N pulses (each maps to a minimal worker footprint), mark them ephemeral with TTL ~ 2–10 minutes, allow per-tenant reservation up to configurable cap.
5) Priming actions: on priming grant, instantiate small, pinned cache + one warm worker (thin) under tenant namespace; keep metric of priming ROI.
6) Reclaim/soft-decommit: priority order — revoke idle pulses > ask tenants to degrade model > throttle new requests; log and surface to tenant console with reason codes.

APIs and Controls (sketch):
- POST /pools/{pool_id}/pulse-request { tenant_id, desired_burst_qps, max_duration_s } -> returns { granted: true/false, pulse_id, ttl_s, reason_code }
- GET /tenants/{tenant_id}/priming-status -> { primed: true/false, priming_level, expires_at }
- Admin: PATCH /pools/{pool_id}/sundial-config { default_window_s, max_pulse_fraction, isolation_floor_pct }
- Telemetry: time-series labels: pulse_id, tenant_id, pool_id, event_type (alloc, revoke, degrade)

Operational runbook (short):
- If pulse saturation is causing SLO breaches: increase isolation_floor_pct, reduce max_pulse_fraction, or widen window to smooth spikes.
- If pulses underutilized: reduce prewarm TTL, lower priming threshold, or expand eligibility (enterprise->paid tiers).
- Escalation: mark pool read-only and fail new pulse allocations if a pool-level 99th latency exceeds threshold for > 2m.

Metrics & success criteria (examples):
- Pulse hit rate (priming: requests served with primed cache) >= 60% within month 1 for enrolled tenants.
- Peak-to-baseline throughput served by pulses for eligible tenants >= 2x for bursts <= 5 min.
- Operator-visible incidents related to cross-tenant regressions < 2 per month at GA.

Privacy & compliance notes:
- Priming keeps only ephemeral, non-customer-PII caches; KMS/HSM controls unchanged.
- Audit logs must capture pulse allocation/release events for compliance customers.

Deployment & rollout plan (phased):
- Canary (1 pool): enable read-only telemetry + simulated pulse granting for 2 weeks.
- Beta (small set of customers): opt-in tenants tested with observability and billing flags; measure priming ROI.
- GA: tiered enablement (enterprise first, then paid tiers) + dashboard for pulse usage and incident reporting.

Open questions / risks (working list):
- Optimal pulse sizing: should pulses be kernel-level warmings (very small) or full worker instances? Tradeoffs noted.
- Fairness across tenants when many tenants are eligible simultaneously — do we prefer proportional share or priority queues?
- Predictor model complexity: EWMA vs small ML model — complexity invites maintenance costs but may materially improve hit rates.
- Cost accounting: how to bill ephemeral pulse usage without surprising customers? (percent-of-minute billing? amortized prewarm fee?)

Next steps / action items:
- Engineering: prototype sundial controller + pulse allocator (Spike, 2 sprints). Owner: Marco Li.
- Applied ML: evaluate priming predictor feasibility on 30-day request traces. Owner: Sofia Nguyen.
- Product: finalize entitlement model (which tiers get priming) and draft billing language. Owner: Asha Patel.
- SRE: write alerting rules and a preliminary runbook for pool overload scenarios. Owner: Diego Morales.

Notes / rough simulation results (informal):
- Small sim on mixed workload trace (50 tenants; median qps 2–10) suggests 6% extra warm capacity yields ~45% reduction in 99th latency tail during 1–3 minute spikes when priming used. Results noisy; needs larger sim.

Appendix (examples & pseudo flows):
- Sample pulse rejection reason: "POOL_EXHAUSTED_ISOLATION" (means reclaiming would breach configured isolation floor).
- Example priming TTL policy: initial grant 90s, extend if > 20% traffic persists for two consecutive windows.

This doc is intentionally a working draft — expect refinements to pulse lifecycle and billing model after the first engineering spike.
